To splurge means to spend more money than you normally would, usually on something special, luxurious, or pleasurable — and to do so willingly and deliberately.

It is the act of going beyond your usual budget or spending habit, even if just for once, to enjoy or treat yourself (or someone else) to something a little extra.

There are a few important things packed into this one word:

1. You are spending more than usual.
The word only makes sense when there is a contrast — between what you normally spend and what you are spending right now. Someone who always buys expensive things cannot really "splurge," because splurging means crossing your own usual line.

A person who normally makes coffee at home and then pays $8 for a fancy café latte is splurging. A person who buys that latte every single day is not splurging — it is just their routine.

2. The spending is on something enjoyable or indulgent.
You don't splurge on rent or electricity bills. You splurge on things that feel like a treat — a nice meal, a luxury item, an upgrade, a vacation, a gift. There is always a sense of pleasure or reward involved.

3. The choice is conscious and deliberate.
Splurging is not an accident. You know you are spending more than usual, and you choose to do it anyway. That awareness is part of the word's meaning.

4. There is often a mild sense of "I'm being a little extravagant here."
Splurging carries a slight tone of self-awareness — a feeling like "I'm treating myself today, even though this is more than I'd normally spend." It is not reckless or irresponsible necessarily, but it is a conscious loosening of your usual financial discipline.
The Most Natural Way to Use It

The most common structure is:

splurge + on + [something]

"I splurged on a new pair of shoes."
"We splurged on a five-star hotel."
"She splurged on the tasting menu at that fancy restaurant."

You can also use it without "on" when the context is already clear:

"It was my birthday, so I decided to splurge."
"We don't usually go out for dinner, but last night we splurged."

You can splurge for someone else too:

"He splurged and bought the whole team dinner."

And you can splurge a little or a lot — splurging is not always about a huge amount of money. It is relative to your normal habits:

"I splurged a little and got the larger size."
"They really splurged and rented a villa in Italy for two weeks."

This is important, because words carry emotional colour, not just dictionary definitions.

Splurge is a warm, informal, mostly positive word. It does not sound judgmental or harsh. When someone says "I splurged," they are usually saying it with a smile — a small confession of enjoying themselves. It sounds like a treat, a reward, a celebration.

It is not the same as:

  • Wasting money — wasting implies you got nothing valuable in return, and the tone is negative. Splurging implies you enjoyed it.
  • Squandering — this sounds reckless and foolish. Splurging sounds deliberate and enjoyable.
  • Being irresponsible — splurging does not necessarily mean you can't afford it. It just means you spent more than you usually do.
Register: Where and When This Word Is Used

Splurge is an informal, everyday word. You will hear it in casual conversation, see it in magazine articles, blogs, social media, and friendly texts. You would not use it in a formal essay, a business report, or academic writing.

✅ "We totally splurged on our anniversary dinner!" (casual, perfect)
❌ "The committee splurged on office renovations." (too casual for formal writing)

A Few More Natural Examples to Cement It

"I've been saving all year, so I'm going to splurge on a really nice coat this winter."

"We don't usually order dessert, but tonight let's splurge."

"The hotel was a splurge, but it was absolutely worth it."

"She doesn't splurge often, so when she does, she really goes all out."

"I splurged and upgraded to business class — best decision I've ever made."

To splurge is to deliberately spend more money than you normally would on something enjoyable, with a full awareness that you are treating yourself or others — and typically, a quiet satisfaction about it.
